## Introduction to Living-Donor Liver Transplantation

- Living-donor hepatectomy is a major surgical operation performed on a **healthy person** only for the benefit of a recipient who requires liver transplantation
- **1989**: Strong performed donor left hepatectomy and removed segment IV on the back table before implantation of segments II and III into a pediatric recipient
- **1990**: Tanaka et al. improvised using a **right liver graft** for a pediatric recipient due to unexpected precarious donor left hepatic arterial anatomy
- **1993**: Makuuchi first performed LDLT using **left liver for adults**
- **1996**: Fan performed the first case of **right liver adult LDLT**

## Historical Development of Right Liver LDLT

- The right liver graft initially included the **middle hepatic vein (MHV)**
  - Addressed problems of **small-for-size syndrome**
  - Provided good venous outflow of the right anterior section
- The first seven recipients who underwent right LDLT all had **acute liver failure** before transplantation
  - One died of candidiasis
  - The other six survived
- Subsequently, **semiurgent and elective cases** were performed

## Donor Workup: Overview

- Donor workup is started after indication for LDLT for the potential recipient is established
- The workup helps evaluate whether the donor will be **psychologically and physically healthy** in the long term after recovery from organ donation
- Conducted in a **stepwise manner** — expedience is achieved without omission
- Only individuals of **good health** who have reached the **age of consent** are considered

## Donor Workup: Step 1 — Medical History & Initial Screening

- A **detailed medical history** is taken to identify comorbidities, if any
- **Body mass index (BMI)** criteria:
  - ≥30 kg/m² raises concern for fatty liver and obesity-related comorbidities
  - ≥27 kg/m² for Asians
- **Blood group compatibility** is verified
- Carriers of **HIV, HBV, or HCV** are denied liver donation
- Hepatitis B core antibody positivity does not preclude donation but mandates **lifelong prophylaxis** with lamivudine or entecavir

## Donor Workup: Step 2a — Psychological Assessment

- A **psychological assessment** is performed to verify:
  - The potential donor's **knowledge of the operation** to be performed
  - The donor's **coping abilities**
- The donor should have adequate knowledge of:
  - **Donor and recipient morbidity, mortality, and survival**
  - The **urgency of the situation**

## Donor Workup: Step 2b — Imaging Studies

- **Chest radiographs** and **electrocardiogram** are performed
- **Computed tomography (CT)** of the liver under sodium bicarbonate cover
- **Maximum-intensity projections (MIPs)** of hepatic veins (HVs) and portal veins (PVs) are produced
- **Volumetry of the donor liver** by the Heymsfield method measures:
  - Volume of the right liver
  - Volume of the left liver (for pediatric recipients, segments II and III)
  - Using the MHV as a demarcation line on the plane between right and left liver

## Donor Workup: Step 2b — CT Findings & Anatomic Assessment

- **Attenuation of liver parenchyma** in comparison with spleen on plain film is appraised for detection of fatty change
- **HV anatomy** is determined by:
  - Axial cuts in the venous phase
  - MIPs for easier appreciation
- **Inferior right HVs**: Anticipate either preservation or division at operation
- **Segment IVb HV or segment III HV draining into MHV**: Requires more caudal division of MHV to preserve adequate drainage of segment IV of remnant left liver

## Donor Workup: Step 2b — Arterial Anatomy Assessment

- The **right, left, and segment IV hepatic arteries** are illustrated by **three-dimensional reconstructions**
- Images obtained during the **arterial phase** of CT imaging
- This detailed arterial mapping is crucial for surgical planning and avoiding vascular complications

## Donor Workup: Step 3 — Liver Biopsy

- Liver biopsy is performed in **selective donors**
- Conducted after genuineness and suitability of the potential donor is ascertained
- **Steatosis criteria**:
  - Up to **15%** for right liver donors
  - Up to **20%** for left liver donors
- Higher steatosis levels may compromise graft function and donor safety

## Donor Workup: Step 4 — Informed Consent

- Informed consent is obtained from the **donor and the donor's relative**
- **Donor and recipient morbidity and mortality risks** are stated clearly
- The donor must fully understand the risks and benefits before proceeding
- This is an ethical cornerstone of living donor transplantation

## Side and Size of Graft: Fundamental Principles

- The **graft-to-standard liver volume ratio** is crucial in LDLT
- A ratio of **>35%** is required for predictable recipient success
- **CT volumetry overestimation**: A 20% overestimation of right liver graft size is common
  - Given a conversion factor of **1.19 g/mL**
- The left liver is usually **one-third the size** of the total liver

## Side and Size of Graft: Left Liver Considerations

- For a donor with body size **no larger than the recipient**, the left liver is usually **<35%** of recipient standard liver volume
- For individuals with a **larger left liver/right liver ratio**, the left liver may be large enough for donation
- **Important note**: In left LDLT, gram-to-gram equivalence of graft is **not applicable**
- A left liver graft of the same size as the right is **less efficacious**
  - Probably because the left liver graft is more likely subject to **compression injury** when the recipient's abdominal cavity is not large enough

## Side and Size of Graft: Right Liver Donation Criteria

- For **right liver donation**, the liver donor should have a **remnant left liver of at least 30%** of the total liver volume
- For a **pediatric recipient**, a liver graft of **3% of body weight** is optimal
- The graft size is lowered to **2% of body weight** for older children and teenagers
- A graft of **>5% of body weight** predisposes to hypoperfusion
- In such cases, graft reduction to even a **monosegment** may be required

## Figure 121.1: Volumetric Analysis of Donor Liver

![Figure 121.1](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **CT volumetric analysis** of the donor liver
- The Heymsfield method measures volumes of right and left liver
- **MHV serves as the demarcation line** between right and left liver
- Essential for determining graft suitability and donor safety

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Exposure — Patient Positioning

- The donor is placed **supine** on the operating table
- Care taken to avoid **pressure sores** over:
  - Occiput
  - Heels
  - Sacrum
- The position must be optimal for the **surgeon and first assistant** to face the operative field directly
- Must be unhindered by metal bars of upper hand retractor or fence between surgeon and anesthetist

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Exposure — Incision & Initial Dissection

- Access gained through a **right subcostal incision** with upper midline extension
- The **ligamentum teres** is ligated and divided
- The **falciform ligament** is taken down
- **Bookwalter retractor** (Codman and Shurtleff) used:
  - Two curved blades pull the rib cage laterally and anteriorly
  - Opens up the aperture made by the costal margins
- In donors with **narrow costal angle**, excising the **xiphoid process** may improve access

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Exposure — Intraoperative Ultrasound

- Following careful laparotomy, **intraoperative ultrasonography (IOUS)** is performed
- IOUS studies:
  - Junction of the **left hepatic vein, MHV, and IVC**
  - Relation of **segment IVb HV to MHV** (already known from CT)
- IOUS also registers **flow characteristics** of:
  - Hepatic arteries
  - Hepatic veins
  - Portal veins
- These serve as reference throughout the operation

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Hilar Dissection — Gallbladder & Cystic Structures

- The **triangle of Calot** is dissected
- The **cystic artery** is divided between ligatures
- The **gallbladder** is dissected from its fossa
- The **cystic duct** is cannulated with a **3.5-Fr Argyle catheter** (Tyco Healthcare)
- The cystic duct is then severed at the site of catheter insertion for delivery of the gallbladder

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Hilar Dissection — Biliary Anatomy

- The **peritoneum overlying the right hepatic duct (RHD)** is divided for identification
- A **large metal LigaClip** (Ethicon Endo-Surgery) is put on the liver capsule at the planned line of division of the RHD
  - Placed **3–4 mm away** from the hepatic duct confluence
- **Operative cholangiogram** performed with undiluted contrast under fluoroscopy with a C-arm

## Figure 121.2: Operative Cholangiogram

![Figure 121.2](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- Metal clip marking the planned line of division of the right hepatic duct
- Image quality improved by temporary gentle occlusion of distal common bile duct with an **atraumatic vascular clamp** (Featherlight Bulldog Clamp; Geister)
- **Important**: Clamp must be removed once cholangiogram is finished to avoid devascularization of donor distal CBD

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Cholangiogram Interpretation

- In the **supine donor**, the right posterior sectional duct is demonstrated **first**
- Followed by the **right anterior sectional duct**
- Then the **left ducts**
- A **variant PV anatomy** (but not hepatic artery) is frequently associated with variant bile duct anatomy
- An **infraportal right posterior bile duct** is more common in donors with variant PV anatomy

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Parallax Technique

- The **parallax technique** is executed by **rotation of the C-arm to the right**
- This clarifies the **anteroposterior (AP) position** of the right anterior and posterior sectional ducts
- Also provides the **true AP view** of the biliary system
- A marking is made with reference to the LigaClip on the liver capsule with **diathermy** for the line of division

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Hilar Vessel Isolation

- Hilar dissection continues to isolate the **right hepatic artery (RHA)** and **right PV**
- The space between the **RHA and RHD should not be disrupted**
  - Preserves the RHD blood supply
- To gain entire length of the **right PV**, branches to the **caudate lobe** are ligated and divided
- **Important**: A sizable branch from the right PV may represent vessels supplying **segment VI**, which should be preserved

## Figure 121.3: Hilar Dissection with Vessel Isolation

![Figure 121.3](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- Isolation of the **right hepatic artery** and **right portal vein**
- The branch of portal vein supplying **segment VI was preserved** (arrowhead)
- Demonstrates meticulous preservation of segmental vascular supply

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Inflow Control & Transection Line

- **Temporary right liver inflow control** is performed
- Vascular clamps applied to RHA and right PV
- This marks the **line of transection along Cantlie's line** with electrocautery
- The line on the **inferior surface** of the liver is just to the **left of the gallbladder fossa**
- Joins the planned line of division of the RHD marked earlier

## Figure 121.4: Temporary Hemiinflow Control & Cantlie's Line

![Figure 121.4](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: Temporary hemiinflow control with vascular clamps applied to RHA and right PV
- **Panel B**: Cantlie's line is revealed after temporary hemiinflow control
- The demarcation line guides precise parenchymal transection

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Posterior Mobilization

- The **right triangular ligament** is taken down, leaving the **Gerota fascia intact**
- In a normal donor liver, the **right adrenal gland** can often be freed from the liver with careful dissection using electrocautery
- **Minor bleeding** from right adrenal gland: controlled by **argon beam coagulator**
- **More severe bleeding**: addressed by plication with sutures

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Short Hepatic Veins

- **Short HVs on the right side** of the midline of the IVC are divided between ligatures and plicated as required
- **Inferior right hepatic veins >5 mm** are **preserved for anastomosis** with the IVC in the recipient
- This preservation is critical for adequate venous outflow of the graft

## Figure 121.5: Inferior Right Hepatic Vein

![Figure 121.5](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- The **inferior right hepatic vein** is isolated and preserved (arrowhead)
- Veins larger than 5 mm require preservation for recipient anastomosis
- Smaller veins can be ligated and divided

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Inflow Occlusion Considerations

- **Continuous inflow control during liver transection is NOT practiced** (unlike hepatectomy for neoplasm)
- The **Pringle maneuver** with intermittent reperfusion:
  - Adopted by some centers
  - Has been shown to result in **less blood loss**
  - However, the difference **did not reach statistical significance**
- Possible explanations:
  - Bleeding from HV tributaries is **not controlled by inflow occlusion**
  - There is bleeding during the **5-minute reperfusion interval**

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Ischemic Preconditioning Debate

- Potential advantage of Pringle maneuver: **downregulation of apoptosis pathway** by ischemic preconditioning
  - Relevant for grafts with long cold ischemic time
- However, associated with **poorer initial graft function**
  - Shown by a prospective trial in deceased donor liver procurement
- For **adult LDLT**, prolonged cold ischemia should **not be an issue**
  - Graft delivery matches the explantation of the native liver

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Blood Loss Reduction Strategies

- **Low central venous pressure** can be attained through good rapport with the anesthetist
  - Proved effective in reducing blood loss
- **Elevating the head and trunk** by 10–15 degrees
- **Complete muscle relaxation** of the donor
- **Cautious use of ultrasonic dissector**
- These measures are helpful in reducing blood loss **without inflow occlusion**

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Parenchymal Transection Setup

- After mobilization of the right liver from posterior attachments
- A **full-thickness suture** at the liver edge on both sides of Cantlie's line
- Helps open up the transection plane by the **weight of hemostats**
- Placement of **laparotomy pad behind the right liver** renders the transection plane more vertical
- But not so excessively as to compromise retraction of the liver during transection

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: CUSA Transection Technique

- Liver parenchymal transection started with **electrocautery or energy source** for the first **1–2 cm** of parenchyma between segments V and IVa
- The rest of liver transection done using **Cavitron Ultrasonic Surgical Aspirator (CUSA)**
  - Exposes the **left side of the MHV**
  - Main trunk lies at **two-thirds the depth** from the superior surface of the liver
- **Terminal branches of MHV** may be encountered early at division near gallbladder fossa
  - Can be exposed and traced to main trunk subsequently

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: CUSA Settings

- **Frequency**: 23 kHz
- **Amplitude**: 60% for normal donor liver
- **Irrigation**: Normal saline at about **4–6 mL/min**
- The liver parenchyma is disrupted by **cavitation of the aerosol**
- **Lower amplitudes**: Operator tends to bring instrument into direct contact with liver parenchyma
  - Will damage small, friable vessels
- **Suction**: Set to moderately high level, just enough to provide clear operative field

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Vessel Management During Transection

- **Electrocautery incorporated into CUSA** allows diathermy of vessels **<1 mm** in diameter
- If **segment IVb HV inserts into MHV**:
  - Transection is **stopped** to preserve this vein
  - Essential for **adequate drainage of left liver**
- **Identification of segment 4b HV** is facilitated by early and complete exposure of full course of MHV

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Hilar Plate Management

- At the liver hilum, the **right portal pedicle containing RHD** is dissected
- **Minimal use of CUSA** in this area
  - Excessive use may **denude RHD from its blood supply**
- The line of division already marked and verified by operative cholangiogram is followed
- Any RHDs are severed with **scissors tangential to the transection plane**
  - Which is often quite horizontal

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Biliary Stump Repair & Verification

- The **RHD stump** is repaired by **6/0 polydioxanone continuous suture**
- An **operative cholangiogram** is performed to confirm:
  - Patency of the **left bile duct**
  - Patency of the **main bile duct**
- This verification step is critical to prevent biliary complications in the donor

## Figure 121.6: Operative Cholangiogram Confirmation

![Figure 121.6](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- Operative cholangiogram confirms **patent left and main ducts**
- Ensures no inadvertent injury to donor biliary system
- Critical quality control step before graft delivery

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Caudate Lobe & IVC Exposure

- Liver parenchyma **dorsal to the MHV** and the **caudate lobe** are transected until the **IVC is exposed**
- Lifting up of the **caudate lobe** with a cotton-tape or right-angled forceps facilitates transection
- Care must be taken to dissect in a **definable plane** between the liver capsule and the IVC

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Graft Delivery Timing

- To have **short cold ischemic time**, the graft is **not delivered until the recipient is ready** for explanting of the native liver
- Graft delivery starts with:
  - Application of clamp onto **proximal RHA**, distal to segment IV hepatic artery
  - RHA divided with scissors
  - **Right PV divided** between vascular clamps, applied at right angle to course of main PV

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Hepatic Vein Division

- The **MHV, RHV, and if present the inferior RHV** are controlled with the **vascular stapler (TA 30; Tyco Healthcare)** before division by scissors
- **PV stump repair**: To avoid stricture, the right PV stump is sutured in a **transverse manner**
  - Using **6/0 Prolene continuous back-and-forth sutures**

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Biliary Leakage Check

- **Biliary leakage and patency of remnant LHD** are checked with:
  - **Intraoperative cholangiogram**
  - **Dilute indigocarmine instillation**
- The indigocarmine in the bile ducts must be **flushed away by normal saline**
- The **cystic duct** is ligated with **2/0 Vicryl**

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Remnant Liver Stabilization

- The **remnant left liver** is maintained in anatomic position by **reconstitution of the falciform ligament** with nonabsorbable sutures
- The **healthy part of round ligament** is also anchored onto the abdominal wall by nonabsorbable suture
- **Purpose**: Prevents the left liver from rotating into the right subphrenic cavity
  - Which could cause:
    - Kinking of the left hepatic vein
    - Liver congestion
    - Liver failure

## Figure 121.7: Remnant Left Liver Stabilization

![Figure 121.7](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- Remnant left liver is prevented from dropping into the right subphrenic space
- Achieved by **suturing the falciform ligament**
- Critical step to prevent postoperative venous outflow obstruction

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Final Checks & Closure

- **Patency of vessels** is verified with **IOUS**
- The **hepatic flexure of the colon** and corresponding portion of **greater omentum** are allowed to ascend into the right subphrenic space
  - Prevents adherence of small bowel to transection surface of remnant left liver
- Care must be exercised to **prevent small bowel going around the hepatic flexure** into the right subphrenic cavity
- The abdomen is closed **without drainage**

## Donor Right Hepatectomy: Outcomes & Experience

- Outcomes of donor right hepatectomy (including MHV) have **improved with accumulation of experience**
- In a consecutive series of **200 donor right hepatectomies**:
  - All including the MHV
  - Operation time was **shortened**
  - Blood loss **decreased** with maturity of techniques
- The skill is **transferable to newer surgeons**
- Good surgical outcomes achieved under guidance from experienced surgeons

## Inclusion of Middle Hepatic Vein: The Controversy

- An area of **ongoing controversy** in right LDLT is whether or not to include the MHV
- **Deleterious effects of no drainage** to segments V and VIII include:
  - Severe venous congestion
  - Necrosis of these segments
- The decision to **exclude the MHV** requires demonstration of **collaterals** between segment V and VIII tributaries and the RHV

## Inclusion of Middle Hepatic Vein: Institutional Algorithms

- **Kyoto University algorithm** — include MHV when:
  - Graft is **MHV dominant**
  - Graft-to-recipient weight is **<1%**
  - Remnant left liver is **>35%** in all cases
- **Chang Gung Memorial Hospital** — includes MHV when:
  - Graft to estimated standard liver volume is **≤50%**
  - Segment V and VIII HVs are **large** and RHV is **small**
- **Tokyo University**: Observed congestion of segments V and VIII after temporary clamping of RHA before determining venous interpositional need

## Inclusion of Middle Hepatic Vein: Authors' Approach

- The authors **include the MHV in all right liver grafts**
  - For **simplicity and familiarity** of the technique
- Irrespective of venous drainage pattern of segment IV of remnant left liver, the **segment IVb HV is preserved**
- **Utmost care** needed for its preservation when it drains into the MHV
- On the back table, **outflow capacity is guaranteed** by **venoplasty of the MHV and RHV into a single cuff**

## Inclusion of Middle Hepatic Vein: Venoplasty Benefits

- Venoplasty allows:
  - **More expedient HV-to-IVC anastomosis**
  - **Higher outflow capacity** of the right liver graft
- This technique has become a standard part of the authors' protocol
- Ensures optimal graft function and recipient outcomes

## Donor Left Hepatectomy: Incision & Exposure

- For a donor with **low body mass index**, an **upper midline incision** can provide adequate access
- The **left coronary ligament** is taken down
- Adequate mobilization of the left liver requires division of the **ligamentum venosum (Arantius ligament)** between ligatures

## Figure 121.8: Upper Midline Incision for Donor Left Hepatectomy

![Figure 121.8](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: Upper midline incision for donor left hepatectomy
- **Panel B**: Adequate exposure for hilar dissection and liver transection gained by widening the aperture of the costal margin
- Less invasive approach for appropriately selected donors

## Donor Left Hepatectomy: Biliary Marking & Cholangiogram

- The **LHD**, which may have a short extrahepatic course, is marked by a **large metal clip**
- The planned line of division is **verified by cholangiogram** under fluoroscopic guidance
- **Special attention**: Identify an insertion of the **right posterior sectional duct into the LHD**
  - In this situation, the LHD can only be divided to the **left of the right posterior sectional duct**

## Figure 121.9: Operative Cholangiogram for Left Hepatic Duct

![Figure 121.9](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- Operative cholangiogram with a large metal clip marking the planned line of division of the left hepatic duct
- Demonstrates the importance of identifying variant biliary anatomy
- Prevents inadvertent injury to right posterior sectional duct

## Donor Left Hepatectomy: Hepatic Artery Considerations

- The **middle hepatic artery (MHA)** should be **preserved** when it arises from the **LHA**
- An MHA that is **not large** and arises from the **RHA** can usually be **sacrificed**
  - Segment IV will be supplied adequately by **collaterals from the LHA**
- A **replaced LHA arising from the left gastric artery** allows a good length of isolated artery

## Figure 121.10: Replaced Left Hepatic Artery

![Figure 121.10](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: CT with reconstruction of hepatic arteries showing replaced LHA
- **Panel B**: The replaced LHA is visible in the lesser omentum (arrowhead)
- **Panel C**: The replaced LHA is isolated and preserved (arrowhead)
- GDA = Gastroduodenal artery; MHA = Middle hepatic artery; RHA = Right hepatic artery; SMA = Superior mesenteric artery

## Donor Left Hepatectomy: Inflow Control & Transection

- **Temporary inflow control** of the LHA and PV by vascular clamp reveals **Cantlie line**
- Liver transection is to the **right of the MHV** by CUSA
- **Caution**: A **low insertion of segment VIII HV into MHV**
  - This segment VIII vein should be **preserved** for venous outflow of right anterior section of remnant right liver
  - Inadvertent damage results in **torrential bleeding**

## Donor Left Hepatectomy: Comparison with Right Hepatectomy

- When compared with donor right hepatectomy (also including MHV):
  - **Blood loss is more significant**
  - **Operation time is longer**
- Likely the result of a **larger liver transection surface**
- The technical complexity reflects the anatomical challenges of left-sided resection

## Segment II and III Donor Hepatectomy: Overview

- Generally, **exposure and hilar dissection** are similar to donor left hepatectomy
- After isolation of the **LHA and left PV**, an **operative cholangiogram** is obtained
- A **large metal clip** marks the planned line of division of the LHD
- **Special attention**: Location of the **right posterior sectional duct**, which may insert into the LHD

## Segment II and III Donor Hepatectomy: Arterial & Parenchymal Management

- If the **MHA supplying segment IV arises from the LHA**, and enough length is distal to it, it can be **preserved**
  - Otherwise, it is **sacrificed**, and the entire LHA is included in the graft
- An MHA arising from the **RHA is most favorable** and need not be isolated
- The liver transection line is about **1 cm to the right of the falciform ligament**

## Segment II and III Donor Hepatectomy: Segment IV & Caudate Management

- The **pedicles supplying segment IV** are:
  - Isolated
  - Ligated
  - Plicated before division
- The **caudate lobe** is often **not included** in the graft
  - Because the upper abdomen of the recipient often has **limited space**
- The **caudate vessels and bile ducts** are ligated, divided, and plicated if needed

## Anatomic Anomalies: Portal Vein Variations

- Besides inadequacy of size and proportion, **anatomic anomalies** may preclude liver donation
- **Contraindication**: When a **major segmental branch of the right PV arises from the left PV intrahepatically**
  - Both right and left hepatectomy become too hazardous
- **Trifurcation of PV branches** (if extrahepatic): Donor operation is still feasible

## Figure 121.11: Portal Vein Trifurcation Management

![Figure 121.11](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: CT reconstruction showing separated right anterior and posterior portal vein branches
- **Panel B**: **Venoplasty** of right anterior and posterior PV branches
- **Panel C**: **Interpositional portal vein** from recipient sutured to right PV branches
- These reconstructions are done on the back table

## Anatomic Anomalies: Hepatic Vein Variations

- The **segment III or IVb HV** could at times drain into the MHV
- **MHV-to-RHV venoplasty** is still feasible in most cases
- Only with a **very caudal insertion** of segment III and IVb HV to the MHV:
  - The MHV and segment VIII HV need to be divided caudally
  - To preserve venous outflow of segment III and segment IV of remnant left liver

## Figure 121.12: Segment III & IVb Hepatic Vein Drainage

![Figure 121.12](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: CT showing segment III and IVb hepatic vein draining into MHV
- **Panel B**: Segment III and IVb hepatic vein is **preserved during liver transection** (arrowhead)
- **Panel C**: **Venoplasty** of right, middle, and inferior right hepatic veins into a single cuff

## Figure 121.13: Low Insertion of Segment III & IVb Hepatic Veins

![Figure 121.13](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: Low insertion of segment III and IVb hepatic veins to MHV
- **Panel B**: Isolation of segment VIII, III, IVb, and middle hepatic veins
- **Panel C**: Merging of segment VIII and MHV by venoplasty using 6/0 Prolene
- **Panel D**: Single-cuffed segment VIII and MHV merged with Gore-Tex interpositional graft, then merged with RHV
- **Panel E**: Reconstruction with deceased donor iliac artery graft

## Anatomic Anomalies: Biliary Tract Anomalies

- **Biliary tract anomalies** occasionally render a liver graft unsuitable
- Example: **Multiple small branches** in the biliary system may complicate reconstruction
- Careful preoperative imaging and intraoperative assessment are essential

## Liver Graft Back-Table Procedure: Timing & Initial Flushing

- To shorten cold ischemic time, the right liver graft is **not delivered until recipient is almost ready** for graft implantation
- Once delivered, the graft is flushed with **three times the graft volume** of cold **HTK solution** (histidine-tryptophan-ketoglutarate)
- Flushing performed while immersed in an **ice-sludge basin** on the back table

## Liver Graft Back-Table Procedure: Portal Vein Cannulation

- The **right PV is cannulated** and adapted to the vein wall with **fingers and not ligature**
- **Separate right anterior and posterior PVs** require **simultaneous flushing with two cannulae**
- This technique ensures complete flushing of the entire graft without intimal damage

## Figure 121.14: Graft Flushing Technique

![Figure 121.14](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: Flushing of right liver graft with HTK solution, adapting nozzle of cannula to right PV with fingers
- **Panel B**: Simultaneous flushing through right anterior and posterior PVs
- **Panel C**: Careful cannulation and flushing of the right hepatic artery
- Avoids inadvertent damage to artery intima which can result in unrecoverable graft loss

## Liver Graft Back-Table Procedure: Arterial & Biliary Flushing

- The **RHA is flushed** with **100 drops of HTK solution** through a **21-Fr angiocatheter** by gravity
- **Critical warning**: Inadvertent damage to the artery intima can result in **unrecoverable graft loss**
- The **right anterior and posterior sectional ducts** are also flushed with cold HTK solution
  - Minimizes duct damage during preservation

## Liver Graft Back-Table Procedure: Venoplasty Technique

- The graft is **weighed** and transferred to another basin with cold HTK solution
- **Venoplasty of the MHV with the RHV** of the graft is then performed
- Even though the MHV and RHV are often at a distance of up to **2 cm**, they can be **drawn together** for fashioning of a single venous cuff

## Figure 121.15: Hepatic Vein Venoplasty

![Figure 121.15](Volume_2_CHAPTER_121.pdf)

- **Panel A**: Right and middle hepatic veins with a significant distance
- **Panel B**: Merging of right and middle hepatic veins into a **single triangular cuff** with minimal trimming
- This venoplasty allows for expedient and high-capacity outflow anastomosis

## Liver Graft Back-Table Procedure: Venoplasty Length Considerations

- Often misled by planar schematic drawings, some have a false perception of **inadequate length** of MHV wall portion for anastomosis to IVC
- In practice:
  - The **IVC is tubular**, with a venotomy made over the RHV stump
  - It faces the venoplasty of the MHV and RHV
  - The portion of recipient IVC **between the RHV and MHV** makes up for the deficit in length
- This preserves the segment IVb HV for venous drainage of remnant left liver

## Left Liver & Segment II-III Graft Venoplasty

- For the **left liver graft** and **segment II and III graft**:
  - If the MHV and segment II and III vein are separate
  - They are merged into an **equilateral triangle with a single cuff**
  - Apex point to the left by venoplasty
- This facilitates **HV-to-IVC anastomosis** in the recipient

## Left Liver Graft: Special Reconstruction Cases

- Only with a **very low insertion of segment IVb HV to MHV**:
  - The MHV is divided **caudal to the former**
  - The MHV is reconstructed with **artificial vascular graft** or deceased donor vessels
- The **iliac vein is preferred** for ease of handling
- The segment VIII HV and MHV could be reconstructed with **iliac artery branches** and common iliac artery for anastomosis with RHV

## Donor Postoperative Care: Overview

- Donor hepatectomy (both right and left) is a **major surgical procedure** on a healthy volunteer
- **Meticulous postoperative care** should be provided by healthcare professionals
- Postoperatively, the donor is transferred to the **intensive care unit**
  - Close monitoring of **hemodynamics** and **respiratory function**

## Donor Postoperative Care: Recovery Protocol

- **Early mobilization** and institution of **chest physiotherapy**
  - Minimize risks of **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** and **chest infection**
- **Infiltration of wound by local anesthetic** before wound closure
  - May reduce wound pain and need for narcotics
- The donor receives a **6-week course of proton pump inhibitor** for peptic ulcer prophylaxis

## Donor Postoperative Care: Special Considerations

- **Female donors** receiving **hormone replacement therapy** and those taking **oral contraceptives**
  - Require **aggressive prophylaxis against DVT**
- These patients are at higher risk for thromboembolic complications
- Appropriate anticoagulation and early mobilization are essential

## Donor Mortality and Morbidity: Safety as Foundation

- **Donor safety is fundamental to LDLT**
- As application of LDLT has extended:
  - From child to adult
  - From left liver to right liver
- The **dilemma between recipient success and donor risk** has been highlighted
- The reported overall **complication rate of donors** is about **20%**
  - Has been reported as high as **67%** in one series

## Donor Mortality and Morbidity: Mortality Statistics

- A **unified system of complication reporting** may narrow the reported range
- Although **even one donor death is too many**, there are at least **19 known donor deaths**
- Estimated mortality:
  - **Donor right hepatectomy**: 0.1%
  - **Donor left hepatectomy**: 0.1% (implied, though text is truncated)
- Mortality is **lower in multicenter series in Japan**

## Donor Mortality and Morbidity: Risk-Benefit Analysis

- In achieving a **5-year recipient survival rate of 80%**:
  - It takes **one donor life to save 160 recipients**
- **Quality of life changes** of the donor in comparison to predonation state are less tangible
- The **long-term biologic consequences** of donor hepatectomy are **not fully known**
- Nevertheless, decreases in:
  - **White cell count**
  - **Platelet counts**
  - **Elevation of liver transaminases**
- Are demonstrable even **2 years after right liver donation**

## Conclusion: Ethical Foundation

- Although **donor mortality after LDLT remains a reality**:
  - Reducing donor mortality and morbidity
  - Improving recipient survival
  - Strengthen the **justification for LDLT**
- With accumulated experience, a **smaller liver graft suffices** in saving a recipient's life
- Thus, **left LDLT becomes more applicable**
- However, **reducing donor risk should not increase recipient mortality**

## Conclusion: Professional Responsibility

- Donor hepatectomy is an **ethical challenge**
  - Once viewed by medical community and society with caution and skepticism
- Donor procedures can only be **partially justified** by the benefit to a recipient who has **no other treatment options**
- **Our common ground**:
  - Commitment to provide care of the **highest standard** to the living liver donor
  - Perform donor operations in **experienced centers**
- This is the only way to:
  - Maintain the **highest quality**
  - **Decrease donor mortality and morbidity**
